terms.definition: The developer has met the city at a pre-development conference to talk through a proposal, but hasn't filed a building permit. A proposal, not a commitment: many change or never go ahead.
A building permit application is on file and the city is reviewing the plans.
The city has approved or issued the building permit. Construction may not have started yet.

Work is probably under way: the building permit is issued and trade permits (electrical, plumbing, mechanical) have been issued since. The city's public records don't include inspections, so this is an estimate.
Every building permit in the project has been finaled.
Marked by hand when a project has clearly stopped.
What the city calls units or dwelling units. Each apartment, condo, townhouse or house counts as one home.
Homes in projects that have applied for a building permit, been approved or are under construction. This is the headline number on the Stats page; proposals at pre-application are counted separately.
Homes in projects still at pre-application: a developer has met with the city, but no building permit has been filed. Many proposals change or never go ahead, so they're kept out of the main total.
Totals include only projects with a reported unit count, so the real numbers are higher. That's why headlines say "at least."
On the map, a project whose number of homes isn't known yet. It adds nothing to the totals until a count turns up in the city's reports.
A project's homes divided by the combined area of its county parcels. A rough measure of density: a site can include land that won't be built on.

A bus stop where at least one route runs every 15 minutes or better in one direction between 10 a.m. and 2 p.m. on weekdays, from Spokane Transit's schedules. Distances are straight-line from the project's map point.

The city's zones grouped for the filters and charts: residential, centers and corridors, commercial and mixed use, downtown, and industrial. The zone codes themselves (R1, RMF, CC2 and so on) are the city's.

Washington's term for buildings about the scale of a house that hold two or more attached, stacked or clustered homes: duplexes through sixplexes, townhouses, stacked flats, courtyard apartments and cottage housing (RCW 36.70A.030). A house with an ADU doesn't count.
Attached homes side by side, each with its own entrance at ground level. Often each sits on its own small lot so it can be sold separately (a unit lot subdivision).
A cluster of small houses around a shared green or courtyard.
A second, smaller home on the same lot as a house, attached or detached: a backyard cottage, a garage apartment or a basement unit.
New homes made inside an existing building, such as offices turned into apartments, or added onto one.
Senior housing, assisted living and other group living, where residents may share meals, services or common rooms.
Divides a lot into small "unit lots", one per townhouse or cottage, so each home can be sold separately while the site is reviewed as one development.
A way of owning homes, not a kind of building: each home is owned separately and the shared parts are owned in common. Condo projects here are sorted by their building type.
An early meeting where a developer walks city staff through a proposal before applying for permits. It's a conversation about an idea, not an application.

Review under Washington's State Environmental Policy Act. Larger projects file an environmental checklist and get a city decision on their impacts before permits are issued, often with a public comment period.
Spokane's Design Review Board looks at how larger projects in some areas, such as downtown, fit their surroundings and makes recommendations before permits are issued.
A permit to use an existing building for something new, such as turning offices into homes.
The city's review of public works a private project builds, usually streets, sidewalks, and water and sewer connections.
Divides a lot into a small number of new lots. "Final" is the last step, after which the new lots are recorded with the county.
Moves the line between neighboring lots without creating new ones. The city calls it a boundary line adjustment.
A permit to move earth and prepare a site before building.
Separate permits for electrical, plumbing and mechanical work. This map reads them as a sign that construction has started.
The application is in, but review hasn't started or is waiting on something.
City staff are checking the plans against the codes. "Extended" means the city has allowed more time.
The city has asked for changes to the plans before review can go on.
The plans have passed review. The permit is usually issued once fees and any remaining conditions are met.
The city has issued the permit, so the work it covers can go ahead. "Extended" means the city has allowed more time.
The work under the permit has passed its final inspection. The city's public records don't give the date.
Final, with a certificate of occupancy: the building can legally be lived in.
An approved plat or lot change is being recorded with Spokane County.
The city has closed the record. That can mean the work is done, or that the application expired or was withdrawn.
